title: As midterms approach, new poll finds that few Americans trust campaigns or Trump
description: Americans are more skeptical of government information than they were a few years ago, with majorities now saying they have little or no trust in federal government information about elections and pol...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Americans are more skeptical of government information than they were a few years ago, with majorities now saying they have little or no trust in federal government information about elections and politics, foreign affairs or the environment, a new poll finds.

The survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and USAFacts shows that while mistrust of government information has grown since 2024, it's also higher than it was at the end of President Donald Trump's first term, underscoring how his recent attempts to dismantle parts of the federal bureaucracy may have affected public confidence in the executive branch, particularly among Democrats.

Those suspicions extend to the results of the coming midterm elections. Only 34% of U.S. adults trust government certifications of election results "a great deal" or "quite a bit," which is down slightly from 40% in 2024. Certification is a typically routine process in which local and state officials confirm the vote count, but it's become politicized since Trump lost the 2020 presidential election.

Trust in government information has also become more partisan since Trump's first term, the survey found.

"It's pretty hard to trust anything that's being communicated," said Shannon Ingram, 46, a Democrat who lives in Maryland, pointing to shifting health recommendations as an example of "questionable" government information she's seen since Trump regained office. "There is a significant amount of bias, and it comes from the people who are authoring the content."

About 6 in 10 U.S. adults have low trust in information from the federal government about the environment, foreign affairs, elections and politics, abortion or immigration — saying they trust it "only a little" or "not at all."

Mistrust in what the federal government says has risen at least slightly on nearly every topic that was asked about in an AP-NORC/ USAFacts survey from 2019. That includes education — which has risen from 37% in 2019 to 53% now — with a 9-percentage point spike in the last year.

The findings come after a year and a half of upheaval in the executive branch. Trump began to dismantle key parts of the federal bureaucracy soon after entering the White House for the second time, moving to end longstanding programs and shutter entire agencies.

Since then, thousands of federal employees have been fired or left their jobs, substantially reducing the ranks of the government statisticians and leading experts to warn about risks to data quality.

Shifting regulations and recommendations have also led to dramatic changes in government policy. Recent changes to longstanding health advice have put doctors and medical organizations at odds with the Trump administration on vaccination recommendations. Earlier this year, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded a scientific finding that has underpinned government action to fight climate change for more than a decade.

Jeremy Cove, a 44-year-old Republican from Missouri, trusts the Trump administration's guidance on matters like vaccines, but he disagrees with their assertion that climate change is not happening, or that humans are not contributing to it.

"I love Trump; I voted for Trump, but some of the things he's doing just makes me distrust more," Cove said. "Stuff like renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America, it just makes you think about what their priorities are. Then you realize it's not what it should be, which in turn, makes you distrust even more."

The gap between Republicans' and Democrats' trust in government information is much wider than it was during Trump's first term, a shift that first began to appear under former President Joe Biden.

Democrats were generally less likely to trust government information in Trump's first term, but not dramatically more than Republicans. That shifted when control of the White House changed hands. Republicans' mistrust in government information rose while Biden was president and fell after Trump took office. Meanwhile, Democrats' doubts declined under Biden and spiked when Trump regained power.

For example, 61% of Democrats now have low trust in information about the federal budget, compared with 42% of Republicans, while 60% of Democrats have low trust in information about crime, compared with only 32% of Republicans.

Larry Haith, a 76-year-old Republican from Idaho, says he tends to trust the federal government — though, he acknowledges that it can vary based on the current administration.

"Generally speaking, I've got more confidence in the federal government today than I've had in years," he said.

Independents, meanwhile, became more mistrustful of government information under Biden and haven't shifted under Trump.

The only issue without a substantial partisan divide in the new survey is vaccination recommendations and safety: about 6 in 10 Democrats, Republicans and independents trust the federal government on vaccination recommendations and safety "only a little" or "not at all."

As the 2026 midterms approach, public concern about the accuracy of the election results is widespread. Just under half of U.S. adults are "extremely" or "very" concerned the federal government will publicly discredit or question election results, tamper with election results, or pressure state election officials to change how they certify or report results.

Over the past few months, Trump has repeated long-debunked allegations of mass voter fraud in the 2020 election, attempted to place new restrictions on mail voting in time for the midterms and pushed Congress to enact a proof-of-citizenship requirement to register and vote. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has also warned state officials that they could lose funding or face investigations if they fail to go along with Trump's election security demands.

At the same time, few Americans trust the information they get from political campaigns. Only about 1 in 10 U.S. adults say the Democratic Party or Republican Party campaign messages are "always" or "often" based in factual information.

In a sign of how deep the mistrust runs, only about one-quarter of Democrats trust their party's campaign messages to be factual at least "often," while a similar share of Republicans say this about their party.

Less than half of Democrats, 44%, trust government certifications of election results "a great deal" or "quite a bit," a substantial decline from 65% in 2024.

Even with Trump back in the White House, though, Republicans haven't seen a similar increase in confidence. Only 29% of Republicans have high trust in government certifications of election results, up just slightly from 2024.

Trust in other sources of information about election outcomes — such as national news outlets or cable news networks — is also low overall.

Kim Murza, a Democrat from Colorado, has faith in the country's ability to run fair elections but blames the Trump administration for eroding Americans' trust in the process.

"My concern is more about what the current administration is doing," said 45-year-old Murza. "I think they are doing whatever they can to try to put that distrust in people's minds."

The AP-NORC/ USAFacts poll of 1,036 adults was conducted July 29 to Aug. 10 using a sample drawn from NORC's probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 4.1 percentage points. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 6.4 for Republicans overall and plus or minus 6.0 for Democrats overall.

title: Kelsey Grammer says Trump may go down as one of the best presidents
description: While Trump’s approval ratings remain underwater, 'Frasier' star Kelsey Grammer offered a more favorable assessment in a recent interview.
fullText:
As President Donald Trump's unpopularity with the American public continues to be reflected in approval polls, Kelsey Grammer has a much rosier outlook, saying in a recent interview that the president will be remembered as one of the best in U.S. history.

In a recent interview with the British talk radio station LBC, the Republican "Frasier" star said Trump loved America and predicted the president will "probably" be remembered as one of the best leaders in the country's history.

"Because nobody really stood up for America in quite some time in the presidency," Grammer said.

Grammer, 71, also praised how he perceives Trump responds to critics.

"He says if somebody comes at him, if they come at him with hate, which they really have done, he just sends it right back at them," he said. "And I think that throws them off."

Grammer's comments also follow an interview in Us Weekly, published June 24, in which he admitted that he has "wrestled" with the idea of running for political office.

"I would consider it. It would possibly tick that box for me, in terms of the service I feel I should have given to my fellow man – to my fellow countrymen – that I missed in the military," Grammer said. "Maybe (running for office) would be the way to do it."

The "Cheers" actor previously claimed that being a registered Republican is the "worst thing you can be" in the entertainment industry, saying during a February appearance on the Megyn Kelly Show that "I've lost some friends through the last few years, but I've gained others." He added he believes it's "not popular" for people with different political values to find middle ground.

Despite Grammer's prediction of Trump's legacy, recent national polls offer a less-than-stellar outlook for the president's popularity with Americans.

In a new Focaldata/Financial Times poll released over Labor Day weekend, the president hit a new record low, as only 32% of Americans said they approved of Trump's job performance. This performance was three percentage points worse than the same poll done in August.

According to Focaldata/Financial Times, Trump's 32% approval is also the worst the president has seen since the poll began tracking it in May.

Trump's approval with Republicans also slipped by 2 percentage points, down to 72%.

Only days before Grammer's prediction, Trump echoed a similar sentiment as he updated his ranking of U.S. presidents in a post on Truth Social.

The initial ranking appeared on Trump's Truth Social account Aug. 27 and listed the 80-year-old as "The Greatest," with Abraham Lincoln, George Washington, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Thomas Jefferson and Andrew Jackson on the next tier down, labeled "Great."

The newest ranking, posted Sept. 6, added several former presidents who were absent from the first list, including Ronald Reagan, John F. Kennedy, Gerald Ford and George W. Bush, among others. Reagan, long known as a conservative icon by many, was placed in the "Near Great" tier.

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump in negative territory overall:

RealClearPolitics (Sept. 9): 39.6% approve, 57.1% disapprove

New York Times (Sept. 9): 38% approve, 58% disapprove

Silver Bulletin (Sept. 9): 38.4% approve, 58% disapprove

USA TODAY's Gabe Hauari & KiMi Robinson contributed to this report.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

Frances Tiafoe, a Maryland native, defeated Alex Michelsen in a hard-fought four-hour match last night to advance to the semifinals of the US Open. Tiafoe rallied from down two sets and managed to overcome Michelsen, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6(10-6), in the next three sets, finishing victorious. Michelsen and Tiafoe shared a long embrace after the match, as the two are good friends and share mutual respect on the court. A picture-perfect moment for media figures as a black competitor shows compassion to a fellow white American opponent.

Although Tiafoe was American-born, he has often spoken about his parents, who escaped the Civil War in Sierra Leon and fled to the US in 1990. He has often mentioned the sacrifices his parents made for him and his brother, as his father, Constant Tiafoe, worked as a day laborer on a construction crew building the Junior Tennis Champions Center (JTCC) in College Park, Maryland, and his mother, Alphina, worked as a nurse. Their immigrant background left room for MS NOW reporters to tie the Trump administration's reluctance toward migrants into the triumph Tiafoe had Wednesday night.

Morning Joe on Frances Tiafoe advancing in the U.S. Open: “For some reason, some people in the White House hate the story of immigrants coming from places they call shitholes & becoming great Americans, that are great examples for our own children.” pic.twitter.com/6szS2ZdEZq

— Tom Elliott (@tomselliott) September 9, 2026

"For some reason, some people in the White House hate the story of immigrants coming from places they call sh*thole countries and becoming great Americans that are great examples for our own children," Joe Scarborough of Morning Joe said.

"What's the origin of the story? The origin of the story is a country in distant Africa. Whats the fulmination, the culmination of the story? The culmination of the story is in the United States of America, by a young man…look at him, he represents America, that's what America is all about," Mike Barniclesaid.

"The tragedy of the Trump administration, both administrations, is they have spent now a decade together, four years out of office, but a decade running this country down. They pose as great patriots. They pose as if we're going to make America strong again; we're going to bring back America. Nobody has to bring back America; the United States of America is the greatest goddamn country on Earth. People don't travel; they don't realize it, but it is."

The classic Trump slogan from his first presidential campaign, "Make America Great Again," caused nationwide chaos as voters on both sides feuded, visibly dividing states. Any supporter of the United States president is now issued the MAGA tag next to their name, a stamp Barnicle found unnecessary to begin with.

Tiafoe's next matchup is against another American opponent, Ben Shelton. No matter the outcome, the US will be a participant in the 2026 US Open final.

title: Trump says oil prices that spiked because of Iran war likely won't come down until after midterms
description: President Donald Trump said Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after U.S. midterm elections.  Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3%, ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won't come down until after U.S. midterm elections.

Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3%, pushing international Brent crude past the $100 threshold for the first time since July as salvos between the U.S. and Iran escalated.

"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump said. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."

Trump, in an exchange with reporters before traveling to Dallas for the midterm Republican convention, added that he believes Iran will finally relent after the pivotal elections are held in the U.S.

"They're desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon," Trump said. He added, "I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said.

The president at the outset of the war said it would last a matter of weeks. The conflict is now in its seventh month. The U.S.-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20% of the world's petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.

The comments were a striking acknowledgment from Trump about the status of the conflict as his Republican administration faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran grinds on with no conclusion in sight.

Trump last week downplayed the conflict as "small potatoes" even as Republicans expressed concern the war will loom large with voters left navigating elevated gas prices and higher inflation.

The U.S. has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.

Trump's prediction that the war won't be wrapped up until after Nov. 3 comes after Vice President JD Vance last week steered clear of predicting that the conflict would be over by the midterm elections, in which Republicans are trying to hang on to their narrow majorities in Congress.

Vance told reporters he didn't want to set "artificial timelines" for the war's end.

"But when you ask, 'When will this end?' You're asking me a question like, 'When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?'" Vance said. "I think the reality is, I don't know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians."

U.S. benchmark crude on Wednesday stood at around $96 a barrel, and U.S. gasoline prices rose sharply overnight.

The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline ticked up 7 cents overnight t o hit $4.22, now more than a dollar above what it cost at this point last year, according to AAA.

Diesel prices, which can have an outsize impact on consumers because it is used in shipping and production, hit an all-time high Friday and have continued to climb since. The average price per gallon rose to $5.94 overnight, up 9 cents from Friday.

Jet fuel has become so expensive that U.S. and international carriers have cut flights while raising fares and fees.

The latest market gyrations come after the U.S. military reported striking five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship and after attacks by an Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group ignited fires at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.

AP writer Cathy Bussewitz contributed reporting.

title: Trump administration proposes dropping huge swath of immigrants from US census

fullText:
Sept 9 (Reuters) - The Trump administration proposed on Wednesday changing the national census to include only U.S. citizens and permanent residents, a move that could significantly change how much ‌political representation and federal funding each state receives.

The U.S. Census Bureau submitted the proposal just over ‌a year after President Donald Trump ordered its parent agency to craft a new census that would block immigrants in the U.S. ​illegally from being counted. The bureau will conduct the next full census in 2030.

The proposed rule changes would exclude even more immigrants from the census, such as those in the U.S. on a temporary lawful basis. The proposed changes would also eliminate parts of the questionnaire that seek information on race or ethnicity, which have been included ‌since the first census in 1790.

The proposal ⁠is open to public comment for 30 days.

Demography experts and civil rights advocates warn that both changes could warp the data used for drawing congressional and state legislative ⁠districts, enforcing anti-discrimination law and allocating federal funds for public services.

FEDERAL AID, POLITICAL REPRESENTATION AT STAKE

The effort could have "earth-shattering" effects, leaving cities and states that have relatively high immigrant populations with insufficient federal aid and political representation, said Meeta Anand, ​senior ​director of the census and data equity program at the ​Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights.

Census ‌data "undergirds so much of our democracy and our society," Anand said. "So you'll start seeing a very inaccurate picture of our country, and then we're making political decisions, business decisions, investment decisions based on data that are flawed."

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump has long decried the fact that immigrants living in the U.S. illegally are included in the census, which is used to determine how many seats each ‌state gets in the U.S. House of Representatives and state ​legislative districts.

In his first term, Trump tried to add a citizenship ​question to the 2020 census but was blocked ​by the U.S. Supreme Court, which ruled that the federal government had given a "contrived" rationale.

The ‌U.S. Constitution's 14th Amendment calls for political representatives ​to be apportioned based on "the ​whole number of persons in each State."

The administration's effort to omit immigrants in the U.S. illegally and temporary immigrants from the U.S. census comes amid its wider crackdown on both legal and illegal ​immigration across the country.

The Justice Department ‌warned on September 2 that states could lose billions of dollars in welfare funding if they do ​not report all immigrants whom state agencies know to be in the country illegally.

title: Trump asks Supreme Court to revive controversial system used for voter purges
description: President Donald Trump asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to reinstate a controversial citizenship records system his administration has sought to wield for sweeping reviews of state voter rolls.
fullText:
President Donald Trump asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to reinstate a controversial citizenship records system his administration has sought to wield for sweeping reviews of state voter rolls.

Voter roll audits using the Department of Homeland Security data program known as SAVE (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements) have been on hold in most of the country since a lower court found that the administration violated privacy law in how it beefed up the program for voter purges.

Critics of the program argue that it produces inaccurate results wrongly identifying eligible voters as non-citizens and could lead to flawed purges that disenfranchise voters.

Trump has made the program a central tool in his government-wide effort to find proof of non-citizen voting. For at least a decade, Trump has claimed that foreigners are tainting elections – allegations that have been debunked in numerous studies of non-citizen voting that have found it to be a rare occurrence.

US Solicitor General John Sauer argued in the new filing that the "indefensible" ruling by the lower court "threatens the integrity of upcoming elections."

The new request the Supreme Court used comes after the Trump administration is already pressing the high court to also reinstate new US Postal Service mandates proposed by the president for mail voting for the midterms.

Many Republican-led states have been eager to use SAVE to vet their voter rolls for potential non-citizens. But they acknowledge that additional investigation is needed of its results before voters are removed from the rolls.

Voter advocates filed the lawsuit after the Trump administration expanded the program to make it easier for states to use for sweeping voter purges. DHS added new sets of data to the program – like Social Security records – and allowed states to upload their voter lists in bulk. Before the changes, states could only use the data program for individualized checks of a voter's citizenship status.

The legal challengers pointed to Texas' experience using the expanded program last year, putting forward evidence that citizens were wrongly purged from the rolls because of the state's SAVE review.

US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, a President Joe Biden appointee, said in her June ruling blocking it that the "federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote."

The DOJ stressed in its Supreme Court filing Tuesday that the federal government was not to blame for any wrongful removals, arguing that the onus is on election officials to make sure that any purges prompted by SAVE audits followed voter registration laws.

The Trump administration has tried to condition states' access to DHS anti-terrorism grants on states' use of SAVE, among other elections-related requirements. Trump also touted the SAVE system in his July speech on elections, claiming that states that had used it found thousands of non-citizens on their voter rolls. However, some states have said the figures DHS put out at the time were inflated and didn't take into account how several of the voters tagged by SAVE as non-citizens were shown to be citizens upon further investigation.

Currently, a handful of states have been able to continue to use SAVE because of separate litigation in Florida.

title: How Canada decided to hurt its own economy, raise its inflation—and most Canadians approved because they’re so angry at Trump
description: Oxford economists predict Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s retaliatory tariffs will slow economic growth and raise consumer prices.
fullText:
Economists are warning that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's "dollar-for-dollar" tariff strategy could mean some economic pain for the Great White North, but Canadians are so frustrated with the Trump administration they support the move anyway.

Canada implemented retaliatory tariffs of 15% to 50% that took effect on Tuesday and will impact hundreds of U.S. goods, including paper, steel, aluminum, furniture, as well as cheese and seafood. The levies were in response to a breakdown of trade talks between the countries and the Trump administration's piling on of tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods earlier this summer.

But the strategy of imposing steep import taxes on the U.S. could cause a phenomenon similar to what happened to American importers, where Canadians carry the burden of the tariffs. In a report published after Canada announced the tariffs on Aug. 25, Oxford Economics analysts warned that while the retaliatory tariffs may help protect some domestic manufacturers, it will also force Canadian businesses to absorb added business costs and increase consumer prices.

Canada depends on the U.S. buyers for about 70% of its exports, and the U.S. economy is about 13-times larger than Canada's.

Oxford projected that Canada's GDP will likely grow by 0.8% in 2026, but tariffs will reduce growth in 2027 by 0.2% to 0.3% relative to its August baseline calculations. It predicted inflation to increase by about 0.3% compared to the August 2027 baseline.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs will most likely be felt in certain regions of the country, Oxford economists said. For example, Ontario, New Brunswick, and Quebec have the highest concentration of manufacturers impacted by the tariffs and rely the most on U.S. exports. British Columbia meanwhile has the highest percentage of its exports, 6.1%, subject to Section 338 Trump invoked to tax Canadian exports. Alberta, Newfoundland, and Saskatchewan—provinces that produce the most oil—will be less impacted on average.

"Canada's new retaliatory tariffs will help some industries but hurt most and weaken economic growth across the country by raising costs for producers and consumers," economists Tony Stillo and Michael Davenport wrote. "The macroeconomic impacts on Canada will likely be modest, but the regional and sectoral implications will be far more significant."

Even as the economic stakes of Canada's involvement in the trade war escalates, Canadians have supported Carney, who is one of the few world leaders standing up to Trump, in the hopes that the import taxes on the U.S. will mount economic pressure and protect Canadian industry.

title: Incumbent GOP governor rolls to primary victory after keeping Trump at a distance
description: Kelly Ayotte cruised past Republican primary challengers, setting up a high-stakes New Hampshire governor's race against Democrat Cinde Warmington.
fullText:
First-term Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte easily handled her primary opponents Tuesday, setting up a high-stakes general election battle against Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cinde Warmington, who ran unopposed for her party's nomination.

Ayotte defeated Republican challengers Shaun Fife and Bob Wayne McClory as she seeks a second two-year term leading the Granite State.

The former senator and state Attorney General entered Tuesday's primary as the incumbent after winning the governor's mansion in 2024, when Ayotte defeated former Manchester Mayor Joyce Craig and kept the office in Republican hands following the retirement of four-term GOP Gov. Chris Sununu.

Key Swing State Voters To Settle Dueling Senate Primary Fights In Crucial Open-seat Race

Ayotte previously served as New Hampshire's attorney general from 2004 to 2009 before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 2010. She served one term before narrowly losing her 2016 reelection campaign to Democrat Maggie Hassan.

In 2024, following Sununu's decision not to seek a fifth two-year term, Ayotte mounted a political comeback with the outgoing governor's endorsement.

In her first term, Ayotte successfully pushed to roll back portions of the state's bail reform law, arguing the existing system was too lenient on criminal suspects awaiting trial, signed legislation requiring public schools to restrict student cellphone use and pushed penalties for motorists who refuse Breathalyzer tests.

Trump-backed John E. Sununu Breaks With President On Key Issue Ahead Of High-stakes New-hampshire Primary

Meanwhile, her tenure has faced criticism from the left over a state budget that included cuts to state agencies.

Ayotte will take on Warmington, who served on New Hampshire's five-member Executive Council for two terms, during which she was the lone Democrat on the body that works with the governor to approve state measures and helps consider gubernatorial appointments, among its duties. Tuesday marked her second campaign for governor after Warmington lost the 2024 Democratic gubernatorial primary.

Warmington has attacked Ayotte for failing to adequately stand up to President Donald Trump, citing healthcare cuts, tariffs and the war in Iran.

title: Fact check: Trump’s story about being carried away by firefighters after the 9/11 attack
description: President Donald Trump has for years told false or unproven stories about what he supposedly saw and did on 9/11 and soon after. As the 25th anniversary of the terror attack approaches, Trump told ano...
fullText:
President Donald Trump has for years told false or unproven stories about what he supposedly saw and did on 9/11 and soon after. As the 25th anniversary of the terror attack approaches, Trump told another story at the White House on Tuesday — in which he claimed to have been carried away by firefighters amid fears of an imminent building collapse at some point after the attack.

It's possible there are elements of truth in Trump's latest story, versions of which he has told before, but he hasn't provided any evidence for it. And some parts of his Tuesday account — which he delivered at an event honoring 9/11 first responders — are misleading at best. He was miles away from the World Trade Center on 9/11 and was not whisked out of any building near Ground Zero that day.

Asked for evidence for Trump's story or more details about what supposedly happened, the White House did not provide any.

The White House said in an unsigned Tuesday email, "He was a private citizen at the time, not everything he did was documented." Later in the day, spokesperson Davis Ingle pivoted to an attack on the media.

"President Trump spent the morning paying tribute to the heroic first responders who laid down their lives in service to others in the September 11th attacks and honoring their incredible families. The President was relaying his experience of a city reeling immediately after and in the days and weeks after the horrific attacks — and the fact that the failing legacy media is using this to try to attack him is a disgrace and yet another reason why Americans' trust in the media is at an all-time low," Ingle said.

Here's a look at what Trump said Tuesday and what the facts are.

Trump wasn't close to the World Trade Center during the attack or later that day

Trump didn't specify when the firemen supposedly helped him, but by beginning the story by saying he went to Ground Zero "right after this happened," he at the least left open the impression that he was whisked to safety on the day of the attack. But that couldn't have happened because he was miles away, at Trump Tower in Midtown Manhattan, when the attack occurred. A former Trump Organization executive told Politico in 2016 that Trump did not do much out of the ordinary that day.

In a 2016 version of the story, Trump claimed the moment the firemen helped him happened "a couple of days" after the attack.

There's no public evidence Trump was in the 'US Steel building' soon after the attacks

With his comments about how he feared the US Steel building was "coming down on top of us" and about how a firefighter said "gotta get out of here," Trump left open the impression that he was inside an unstable building. But there is no public evidence he was actually in the building he was referring to (better known as One Liberty Plaza in 2001 and still today) in the days after the attacks. Two days after the attack, he was interviewed outdoors in the general vicinity of Ground Zero.

In Trump's 2016 telling of the story, he made clear he wasn't inside when the firemen supposedly lifted and moved him; he said the building that appeared on the verge of collapse was "not so far from us."

There was indeed unfounded panic about One Liberty Plaza, though no proof Trump was swept up in it

In the days after the attack, there were fears that One Liberty Plaza would collapse even as city building officials said it was structurally sound; CNN reported that rescue workers and journalists were evacuated from the building on September 12, 2001, and The Washington Post reported that rescue workers were rushed away again on September 14, 2001.

Trump alluded to a similar situation when he was interviewed on September 13, 2001, telling NBC of workers at Ground Zero: "Every few minutes, a whistle would go off and everybody would just run, because you have all the buildings around it, which are in such a weakened state that people just don't know. And so they just have to take off, and then they come back, and they're working under 50-story buildings that you don't know if they're going to fall down. So it's a terrible thing for the workers and it's a terrible thing for the world, really."

It is possible Trump was personally swept up in one of these moments of panic, too. But there's no proof of that, and he didn't tell NBC that he was talking about himself running.

There's no public evidence Trump had a crew helping with the rescue effort

This time, Trump didn't explicitly say that he or his workers helped to clear rubble or otherwise assisted with rescue and recovery at Ground Zero. But he has made such explicit claims in the past, and this time he immediately thanked "my people" after mentioning the work of rescue and recovery crews. So it's worth noting that he has never presented evidence for his claims that he worked at Ground Zero or organized a group that worked at the site, let alone the 100-strong group of workers he has previously claimed.

"I spent many months there myself, and I never witnessed him," Richard Alles, a retired New York Fire Department official who was a battalion chief on 9/11 and who attended a Trump White House event in 2019, told The New York Times in 2019. Alles told PolitiFact in 2019 that if Trump had sent a crew of 100 workers, "there would be a record of it. Everybody worked under direct supervision of the police and fire department and the joint commander for emergency services."

The Associated Press reported in 2016, "News accounts from days just after 9/11 include references to Trump giving high-fives to police officers and volunteers on their way to the World Trade Center site."

No basis to say One Liberty Plaza 'still creaks'

Trump said, "The truth is it creaked a lot, it creaked. It still creaks." There is no basis for this claim. The One Liberty Plaza office building reopened in October 2001, less than two months after 9/11, and functions normally today.

fullText:
Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children

Veteran documentarian Alex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planet has been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0.

The result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us:

Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving him assistance

At Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers.

In spite of everything, there was something admirable about Musk once

Gibney’s film serves as a reminder that Musk has never been in possession of charm or charisma – the petulant perma-poster retweeting praise is not far from the self-regarding twentysomething start-up bro. But what he did with the funds he earned from selling shares of his first software companies, Zip2, X.com and PayPal, was unusual, Gibney concedes. Where others turned to venture capital, Musk turned to engineering. It’s partially an act, we learn from his ex-wife Justine when she recalls how self-consciously he picked his wardrobe, telling her “I can’t look cool or hip, because I need to look like an engineer”. But in footage of Musk biting his nails with fellow engineers during SpaceX rocket launches his enthusiasm and emotional investment is genuine, and at times infectious.

Musk’s procreation drive is motivated by a fear of civilisational breakdown

Musk has 14 publicly known children, and sources tell Gibney that there are probably more. Some of them were conceived in romantic relationships but more recently the circumstances of their birth seem to have been entirely transactional, via sperm donations to employees of his companies. In a text message to one of his ex-partners, influencer Ashley St Clair, Musk said his desire to have “a legion of children” was driven by a fear of “civil war”. The documentary mostly places the roots of that fear in his South African childhood (in one scene, his father Errol Musk talks with no visible remorse of shooting three intruders in their home). “It’s no doubt he had a traumatic childhood,” Gibney said at a press conference in Venice. “He’s now playing out the trauma on the rest of us.” But, oddly for a man who was long a prominent atheist, the film also hints at a religious dimension to his vision of the apocalypse. The sordid business of negotiating disbursements and NDAs with the mothers of Musk’s children are handled by his right-hand man Jared Birchall, a devout Mormon whom St Clair calls his “henchman” and “demon”.

To Musk, empathy is good in principle but not in action

Recently, Musk has held forth at length about his view that “suicidal empathy” – people who have more empathy for criminals than the victims of criminals, in his view – is behind the decline of western civilisation. Empathy isn’t bad, he says in the doc, it’s just that it’s become too shallow. But interviews in the film raise the question of whether Musk is capable of empathy at all. This is a man who tells his wife that “if you were my employee, I would fire you”, and urges her to tell his estranged trans-daughter Jenna that “I’ll always love her” – and then cuts off her health insurance the next day.

Musk knew with a disconcerting degree of certainty that Trump would re-elected

In the film, St Clair describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she tells Gibney, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before”. He told her that he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix” and that “we have 10,000 lasers in space”. Gibney leaves that comment hanging.

The godfather of AI is worried Musk might rig the next election

Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning British-Canadian computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, used to be friendly with Musk, but the pair fell out after Hinton declined his offer to join the xAI board. In the film, he makes clear that he does not trust Musk to weigh up the risks and benefits of AI responsibly, and there’s more. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” Hinton says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on US citizens. And what Doge did looked like just what you would do.”

title: Irish Open will feel 'different' with Trump visit
description: Rory McIlroy admits this year's Irish Open will feel like a "different" spectacle given US President Donald Trump's anticipated visit during the tournament.
fullText:
Rory McIlroy admits this year's Irish Open will feel like a "different" spectacle given US President Donald Trump's anticipated visit during the tournament's latter stages.

Trump is expected to attend the event - which is being held at his resort in the County Clare village of Doonbeg - this weekend as part of a two-day visit to Ireland.

McIlroy has previously played golf with Trump, who earlier this year praised the Northern Irishman's accomplishments on the course after winning back-to-back Masters titles.

"It's going to be different, but the one thing I'd say is his golf resorts have hosted PGA Tour events, European Tour events, LIV events," McIlroy told BBC Sport NI's Stephen Watson.

"He's a big fan of golf, he's a wonderful supporter of golf. He's got a beautiful property here in Doonbeg - it's the first time I've played it. I wouldn't say it's a true links golf course, it's a bit of an Americanised version of a links course, but it's still a great golf course and should provide a good test for the week.

"It's going to be different with him being here but we're here to play a golf tournament and it's a good golf course and keep our head down and play."

During his long-planned visit to Ireland, Trump will meet Irish President Catherine Connolly and hold a bilateral meeting with the Taoiseach [Irish prime minister] Micheal Martin.

He may also present the Irish Open winner with the trophy on Sunday evening amid a significantly enhanced security presence at the property he purchased in 2014.

"I think the weekend, especially when he's here [will feel different], crowds will be limited," added McIlroy.

"Obviously, there's a lot that goes on. So, logistically, it provides some challenges, absolutely. But at the same time, if he wants to come and watch the Irish Open, who are we to say no?"

'We'll see' - Rahm unaffected by LIV 'turbulence'

Trump set to attend star-studded Irish Open at Doonbeg

Six-time major winner McIlroy headlines a strong field at Doonbeg that also features LIV players such as Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Tom McKibbin.

The 2026 LIV season ended early following the cancellation of its team championship in Michigan amid ongoing uncertainty surrounding the tour's future.

On Tuesday, two-time major winner Rahm was tight-lipped about his future and said he was not fretting about the "turbulence" away from the course.

"It's a hard one - I wouldn't want to be in their shoes at the minute and I think just the headspace that it's taken up with the guys, fighting for money or the contracts or where they're going to be playing over the next few years," said McIlroy, 37.

"It's more like the uncertainty for them and it would be nice I think for everyone just to have a bit of certainty around the game and know what's going on and where certain players are going to be playing.

"I'm obviously glad that I'm not really a part of that and I know what I'm going to be doing the next few years, but for everyone involved it would be nice to have certainty and just sort of move forward."

Like Rahm, McIlroy hopes to join European legends Seve Ballesteros, Bernhard Langer, Nick Faldo and Colin Montgomerie on three Irish Open wins after capturing his second title at the K Club last year.

McIlroy also finished runner-up to Rasmus Hojgaard at Royal County Down in 2024 and the world number two believes he is "more relaxed" playing in front of home crowds having also secured a top-10 finish in last year's Open Championship at Royal Portrush.

"I probably went a few years where I wasn't very proud of how I played in the Irish Open," said McIlroy, whose first Irish Open success also came at the K Club in 2016.

"I sort of struggled to deal with the obligations or the pressure or whatever it was, but I think I'm a little bit more relaxed about it these days.

"It's nice to have been able to win it a couple of times and I think coming back after the year that I've had and winning another Masters...I still feel pressure at times playing golf, but coming back to a home crowd and a home open, that shouldn't be one of those."

McIlroy, who finished the PGA Tour play-offs with back-to-back top-four finishes, begins his title defence at 13:35 BST on Thursday. He has been grouped with five-time major winner Brooks Koepka and European Ryder Cup team-mate Robert MacIntyre.

title: UN agency accused of Hamas ties sees another European nation cut funding

fullText:
Another European nation has stopped funding the U.N. agency that aids the Palestinians. Finland has followed the U.S. and Sweden in halting donations to the terror-tainted agency.

The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), is presently being investigated for ties to the terrorist rulers of Gaza. Finland's Ministry for Foreign Affairs confirmed to Fox News Digital that the agreement with UNRWA would conclude at the end of 2026 but that "As of yet, no decision has been made on what are the international partners through which Finland's support will be channeled next year to meet the acute needs in the region."

Finnish officials did not respond to Fox News Digital's questions about what prompted the change to the country's funding for UNRWA.

Us Urges Donors To Abandon Unrwa Funding As Un Defends Agency's Mission

While other nations still continue to fund UNRWA, President Donald Trump fully banned funding to the organization in February 2025, and Sweden ended funding to UNRWA in December 2024. Sweden redirected aid to other U.N. bodies for its Gaza response.

The future of aid provision in Gaza matters for the Trump administration-backed Board of Peace as it seeks to shape a conflict-free future for the region.

An official affiliated with the Board of Peace reconstruction effort told Fox News Digital that "the international community's concern about UNRWA in Gaza continues to rise and is supported by damning evidence. The Board of Peace has been clear: New Gaza will be both demilitarized and deradicalized, and we will only be working with trusted, credible delivery partners to achieve our goals. We anticipate responsibly replacing UNRWA with vetted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza."

Watchdog Demands Apology After Un Memorial Erroneously Honors Hamas Terrorist

The USAID OIG is investigating about 1,500 members of UNRWA for terror participation, and has referred 108 UNRWA staff to the State Department to suggest they be suspended or excluded from further work with organizations in receipt of U.S. funds.

A senior U.S. official briefed on USAID OIG's ongoing investigation told Fox News Digital that the USAID OIG's "independent findings are prompting several other countries to reassess the stale and conventional thinking that UNRWA is the best and only option to provide aid to civilians in Gaza." The official said that the USAID OIG's "findings also will prevent Hamas and October 7 affiliated staff from circulating across future, more responsible, aid organizations operating in Gaza."

World's Humanitarian System Buckling, 'No Longer Fit For Purpose,' Us-based Researchers Say

UN Watch's Terror Network report claims that about 12% of UNRWA staff in Gaza are members of terror organizations, based on "cross-checking UNRWA employee rosters with Hamas records seized by the [Israel Defense Forces.]"

Executive director of UN Watch Hillel Neuer told Fox News Digital that "Finland's principled decision to defund terror-infested UNRWA will not deprive Palestinians of aid, as it will be redirected through genuine humanitarian agencies such as the World Food Programme that are not systemically infiltrated by Hamas."

He said that "other democracies should follow" the examples of Finland, Sweden, and the U.S. "Contrary to what UNRWA supporters claim, the agency is not 'indispensable' — assistance can and must be delivered through responsible alternatives."

Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, told Fox News Digital that "UNRWA has taken note of the announcement, and they are grateful to Finland for the disbursement of the 2023–2026 funds under the multi-year agreement. UNRWA looks forward to continuing our discussions with the government." He explained that "the Secretary-General continues to encourage member states to support UNRWA's vital work."

Finland's four-year funding was around $23.23 million to UNRWA and will now end after this year. UNRWA did not respond to Fox News Digital questions about Finland's decision.

Neuer said "defunding UNRWA is a prerequisite for deradicalization, the first step in the Gaza peace plan. Far from harming the prospects for peace, dismantling UNRWA is essential to achieving it. For decades, the agency has perpetuated the conflict by teaching generations of Palestinians that their future lies not in building their own society, but in a so-called 'right of return' that would eliminate Israel."

He concluded by noting that USAID OIG and UN Watch's exposes on UNRWA prove that "the agency is unreformable. Nations that genuinely want peace should stop financing this machinery of hate, and invest instead in humanitarian relief, deradicalization and Palestinian self-reliance."

title: Trump approval rating reaches new record low in latest poll
description: Ahead of November’s midterms, President Donald Trump’s approval rating hit a record low in a newly released Focaldata/Financial Times poll.
fullText:
As November's midterm elections loom, President Donald Trump's approval rating continues to struggle, reaching a new record low in a new Focaldata/Financial Times poll released over Labor Day weekend.

The poll, released on Sunday, Sept. 6, found that only 32% of Americans approved of Trump's job performance, a three-point drop from last month's edition and the lowest the president has seen in Focaldata/Financial Times tracking since it began in May.

Trump's slip in the most recent poll comes as his approval among Republicans also dropped by two percentage points to 72%, marking a new low, according to the Financial Times.

The president's continued struggles in the polls come ahead of a vital midterm season as his party seeks to hold slim majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The Focaldata/Financial Times poll was conducted from Aug. 28 to Sept. 2 with 2,178 U.S. adults participating.

As the war on Iran continues to rage past the six-month mark, its effect on the prices of everyday items in the United States has become a point of intense disapproval for the president.

According to the poll, only 17% of respondents approved of Trump's handling of inflation and the cost of living, while a whopping 69% disapproved of the president's performance on the issue.

Americans' unhappiness with Trump's job on the economy comes as gas prices in the United States show no sign of dropping. According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of gas was $4.15 on Tuesday, Sept. 8, up 13 cents from a week earlier and nearly $1 higher than it was at the same time in 2025.

Trump's unpopularity with the American public could prove to bolster Democrats' chances of retaking one or both chambers of Congress in November.

According to the latest Focaldata/Financial Times poll, Democrats lead the GOP by seven percentage points in a generic Congressional ballot. That performance shows a one-percentage-point improvement compared to the same poll conducted in August.

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump in negative territory overall:

RealClearPolitics (Sept. 8): 39.6% approve, 57% disapprove

New York Times (Sept. 8): 38% approve, 58% disapprove

Silver Bulletin (Sept. 8): 38.2% approve, 58.4% disapprove

title: IRS under Trump unlawfully shared taxpayer info with immigration authorities, court rules

fullText:
Sept 8 (Reuters) - A U.S. appeals court on Tuesday upheld an injunction blocking an Internal Revenue Service policy that allowed it to share thousands of taxpayers' ‌addresses with immigration authorities, saying the Trump administration's practice violated federal law.

A three-judge panel of ‌the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled that the IRS last year disclosed roughly 47,000 ​taxpayer addresses to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement under a procedure adopted as part of the administration's efforts to expand immigration enforcement.

The IRS and U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not respond to requests for comment.

Under an agreement between the agencies, the IRS in July 2025 began processing ICE ‌requests for the last known addresses ⁠of as many as 1.28 million people suspected of unlawfully residing in the United States.

The IRS adopted a procedure that allowed ICE to obtain information on ⁠taxpayers if it provided a five- or nine-digit number in an address field, even if that number was not an actual ZIP code.

Groups including the Center for Taxpayer Rights and the Main Street Alliance sued, arguing ​the ​practice was unlawful. A lower-court judge agreed and blocked ​the policy, by which time the IRS ‌had already shared 47,289 records with ICE.

President Donald Trump's administration on appeal contended the ruling hindered federal law enforcement.

"But that's a gripe with Congress, not the court," U.S. Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard said in the appeals court's ruling.

Pillard, like the rest of the three-judge panel, was appointed by Democratic President Barack Obama.

After the Watergate scandal during President Richard Nixon's era exposed abuses of U.S. taxpayers' information, Congress barred ‌the IRS sharing information with other government agencies unless ​they complied with stringent conditions.

Pillard said the procedures the IRS ​under Trump adopted violated federal law in ​numerous ways, including "most egregiously" by not even requiring ICE to provide an actual ‌address for a taxpayer as legally required.

The ​practice, Pillard said, "automates the review ​of millions of records without any individual review or any other means of ensuring compliance with the legal prerequisites to releasing each individual taxpayer's information."

Skye Perryman, whose liberal legal group ​Democracy Forward represented the plaintiffs, ‌in a statement said she was pleased the court "acted to stop this unlawful behavior."

"The privacy ​laws enacted in the post-Watergate era exist to prevent abuses of power just like ​this," she said.

title: Blue Jays Nation Challenges ‘Petulant Child’ Donald Trump After Lake America Update
description: The Toronto Blue Jays were at the center of political debate after U.S. President Donald Trump renamed Lake Ontario amid a trade dispute.
fullText:
The Toronto Blue Jays spent one of their final series of the regular season turning a road stadium into something resembling home games, with fans traveling across the border to support a team fighting for an American League playoff spot.

During Toronto's recent series against the Cleveland Guardians, a matchup that carried major wild-card implications, Blue Jays fans traveled en masse. The Blue Jays won the season series and, in the process, secured an important tiebreaker that could become critical if the teams finish with identical records.

"The Blue Jays hold the tiebreaker over the Guardians after winning the season series earlier this week," Sportsnet noted on Monday. "Both teams have 18 games remaining."

But the Toronto-Cleveland series also carried some political weight as the teams' respective nations engage in a tense trade war with significant rhetorical implications.

Dodgers' Pending $400 Million Free Agent Could 'Gravitate' Toward Angels Contract

The recent Guardians series provided a striking reminder of how many Blue Jays supporters cross the U.S.-Canada border to follow their team.

"If you closed your eyes, you might have thought the Blue Jays were playing at home," Mike Wilner reported for the Toronto Star. "Over a three-game series with huge playoff implications, every Jays' run was met with loud cheers and there were several spontaneous chants of 'Let's go Blue Jays!' that rained down from the seats at Progressive Field in Cleveland, which sits at the corner of Ontario Street and Carnegie Avenue."

That cross-border connection took on a different dimension after President Donald Trump issued an executive order directing the federal government to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

The White House order, signed August 27, directs the Interior Department and Board on Geographic Names to take steps to rename the body of water and update the federal Geographic Names Information System. The order describes the lake as an important American economic and strategic asset.

The decision has drawn attention in Canada, particularly because Lake Ontario is shared by the United States and Canada. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has continued referring to the body of water as Lake Ontario.

And for several Blue Jays fan attending the Cleveland series, the political dispute couldn't be ignored.

Joshua Glass, travelling with a friend who gracefully exited the conversation when he heard what the topic was going to be, doesn't share his fellow fans' hesitance.

"I'm not going to pay attention to the rantings of a petulant child, quite frankly," said Joshua Glass, one Blue Jays fan in attendance in Cleveland, according to Wilner. "It's not going to keep me from going to see my team fight for a wild-card spot. I think the whole thing is a bit ridiculous, but it's not going to prevent me from coming ... I'm going to be here no matter what. Until they close the border, that is."

While the political dispute didn't seem to turn Blue Jays away from supporting their favorite team in Cleveland, several of them indicated that Trump's latest geographic moniker decision did give them second thoughts about visiting the U.S.

"After the whole 'Lake America'/Lake Ontario thing," a fan named Melissa told Wilner. "You kind of get numb to the whole 'We're going to charge you tariffs' and everything like that, but as it just escalates now you just kind of get turned off from wanting to come, but I'm going to love the game."

Member Of Yankees' Legendary World Series Championship Roster Dies

For the Blue Jays, the larger story remains the playoff race. Toronto and Cleveland were separated by the thinnest of margins entering the final stretch, making their season series particularly significant.

And the passionate Cleveland turnout demonstrated that Toronto's fan base remains willing to travel when the stakes rise. With the Blue Jays pursuing a wild-card berth, that support could continue to follow them throughout the postseason chase.

fullText:
US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’

The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.

In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.

It also warned it could undermine “independent journalists” and amount to “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online”.

The statement, made via the US embassy in London, raises the stakes in the plans to give the likes of the BBC, ITV and other established media more visibility on increasingly dominant digital platforms.

Ministers, regulators and public service broadcasters have suggested new rules are needed to counter growing misinformation online as people increasingly turn to less regulated online platforms such as X, YouTube and TikTok.

In a consultation this year, the UK government said it would consider legislating should the platforms not act to prioritise trustworthy content. However, Washington claimed such a plan risked effectively removing the content of “independent journalists” over established outlets.

“Preserving a free, open internet and protecting freedom of expression online are top priorities for the Trump administration,” it said. “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.

“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government-disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal. The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship.”

The administration has asked what safeguards will be in place to ensure “any biases and preferences of UK government officials and third-party organisations” do not influence the plan in ways that disadvantage “independent or minority-viewpoint journalism”.

A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper. We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”

Insiders say any measures would only affect the UK. The US complaint highlights its readiness to fight for the largely US-based tech companies that run the world’s largest digital platforms.

Donald Trump also has a long record of attacking and bypassing the established media, regularly accusing major outlets of “fake news” and biased coverage. He often tries to reach supporters online.

The US president is still engaged in his lawsuit with the BBC over an episode of Panorama in which it spliced together one of his speeches. The BBC has apologised for the edit, but stated the show did not defame Trump.

Social media companies have previously been sceptical about artificially boosting the prominence of traditional media, arguing that it goes against the principle of creator content.

Online content creators have compared the proposals to state control and fear their content would be pushed down the rankings as a result.

Simon Squibb, a UK YouTube creator, said he was encouraged that his concerns were shared by an “entity that I think politicians will listen to”.

“This is a very dangerous potential direction for the UK to go in,” he said. “I’m happy that the USA has stepped in.”

Supporters of the enforced prominence plans have couched them as a way of dealing with misinformation and preserving culturally British content.

However, the government has also been clear that it wants to help public service broadcasters survive the economic turmoil created by the rise of digital platforms, which all media companies are confronting.
