title: Judge indicates Trump pressure campaign could permanently sink Reflecting Pool case
description: Asked whether prosecutors were investigating Hearn, they said they weren't.
fullText:
Former U.S. Olympian David Hearn and his attorneys returned to court to urge the judge who previously oversaw his Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool vandalism case to formally bar federal prosecutors from seeking new charges against him.

In late July, the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office moved to dismiss the criminal case against Hearn in a filing that acknowledged damage to the Reflecting Pool "was the result of flawed installation" and not the work of vandals -- prompting outrage from President Donald Trump.

But the motion from U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro asked the judge overseeing Hearn's case, Todd Edelman, to dismiss the indictment "without prejudice," which would leave the door open for prosecutors to potentially seek to re-charge Hearn.

Hearn's attorneys have argued a series of statements from Trump and other officials in the weeks after Pirro's motion that falsely accused him and others of vandalizing the pool warrants dismissal of the case "with prejudice" -- effectively shutting the door for prosecutors to charge him again.

DOJ seeks to keep door open to re-charge David Hearn in Reflecting Pool case

"U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision [to dismiss Hearn's indictment]," Trump said in an Aug. 7 post on social media.

In Friday's hearing, Judge Edelman pressed an attorney from Pirro's office, Michael Spence, on why prosecutors would object to dismissing the case with prejudice when they've received no evidence thus far suggesting anything Hearn did was a crime.

"I don't know what the future will bring -- none of us do," Spence answered, adding if evidence did ultimately surface, "there's no reason this court should tie the hands of a future grand jury to bring that indictment."

"Where is it gonna come from?" Edelman asked.

"That I don't know," Spence answered.

Former Olympian David Hearn's lawyers say Trump pushing 'false version' of Reflecting Pool case

When asked by Edelman whether prosecutors were still investigating Hearn's conduct, Spence said they were not.

"The U.S. Attorney's Office is not, no," Spence answered.

At one point, Edelman zeroed in on Trump's public comments about Hearn's case and his public suggestions he might fire Pirro if she doesn't revisit her decision to drop the case.

"How do I conclude these statements as anything other than statement by the chief executive urging your office to pursue a prosecution that you have told me is meritless?" Edelman pressed. "Isn't this a pretty unique threat of not just re-prosecution but meritless re-prosecution?"

"I think, Your Honor, it's premature to even get there because there has not -- this case has been dropped. It has not been submitted to a new grand jury for an indictment," Spence replied.

Former Olympian David Hearn's attorneys want Reflecting Pool vandalism case permanently dismissed

Spence argued that even if the government did at some point move to re-charge him, the grand jury process would serve as a kind of protection ensuring he wouldn't be charged based on no evidence.

"How could Mr. Hearn look at this case and make that conclusion?" Edelman asked with clear skepticism, noting Hearn was previously indicted in a case the government now concedes was baseless.

"We believed based on the evidence that we had at the time that we had probable cause, and the grand jury agreed that we did have probable cause," Spence answered.

title: Jones stuns Trump to set up final against Selby
description: Jak Jones earns a surprise win against Judd Trump at the British Open, and will face Mark Selby in the final.
fullText:
Jak Jones earned a surprise win against Judd Trump at the British Open and will face Mark Selby in the final.

Jones produced breaks of 95 and 68 on the way to a 3-1 lead before Trump levelled the match at 3-3.

However, Jones knocked in a 59 and a 52 to go 5-3 in front and, after England's Trump missed a green on the colours in a lengthy ninth frame, the Welshman secured victory.

"I started off quite well before the interval and then after that I started missing a few, didn't I?" Jones, beaten finalist in the 2024 World Championship, told Channel 5.

"I can't say I'm in this position a lot so it's a bit different for me compared to Judd."

Meanwhile, Selby came through a hard-fought win against fellow Englishman Liam Highfield, who was playing in his first ranking event semi-final.

Highfield took the opening frame before Selby levelled with an 85 and moved into a 3-2 lead.

A 56 helped Highfield level at 3-3, but Selby took three frames in a row to secure a 6-3 victory and a place in his 40th ranking event final.

"It was a tough match, Liam didn't make it easy for me at all," said Selby, who can climb from fourth to second in the rankings if he wins the title.

"His safety was incredible. I can't remember him playing a poor safety shot all the way through the match."

He added: "To think, when I was starting out, a 16-year-old kid in 1999, if somebody had said I'd get to 40 ranking finals, I'd have said 'no chance'. I'd have been happy to get to just one or two."

fullText:
Sept 5 (Reuters) - A federal appeals court panel rejected the Trump administration's bid to lift a ban on ‌using a federal immigration database to check the accuracy ‌of citizenship records on states' voter rolls.

In a 2-1 ruling on Friday, ​the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia declined to lift a lower court's ban on using the Homeland Security Department's Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements database. The earlier ruling ‌determined that the government ⁠cannot use the system ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which Trump's Republicans ⁠will be defending narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Chief Judge Sri Srinivasan and U.S. Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, both appointed ​to the ​appeals court by President Barack ​Obama, upheld the lower ‌court decision that the SAVE system violates the Social Security Act as it shares millions of Americans' private information. The appeals court judges also noted concerns around the potential for inaccurate citizen information that could lead to people having to prove ‌citizenship to remain registered voters, and ​in some cases could even lead ​to voter registration being ​canceled.

U.S. Circuit Judge Gregory Katsas, an appointee ‌of President Donald Trump, dissented.

A federal ​judge in ​Florida in July ordered the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to resume giving four Republican-led states access to the ​database after another ‌judge blocked it from continuing to use the ​database nationwide.

title: The Venezuelan billionaire the US investigated for money laundering now has a Pentagon oil deal
description: , Marianna Parraga and Gram Slattery CARACAS/MIAMI, Sept 5 (Reuters) - The billionaire who helped broker the Trump administration’s sweeping long-term oil deal with Venezuela was
fullText:
CARACAS/MIAMI, Sept 5 (Reuters) - The billionaire who helped broker the Trump administration's sweeping long-term oil deal with Venezuela was until recently a target of U.S. money-laundering investigations involving funds embezzled from the state-owned oil company PDVSA. Now, after assisting U.S. authorities ahead of the capture of authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro, Alejandro Betancourt is Washington's key partner in an unusual oil agreement with Caracas.

According to last week's announcement, the U.S. gains access to about one-fifth of Venezuela's crude reserves for decades. The Pentagon's ‌Office of Strategic Capital takes a 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), Betancourt's company and a known crude producer in Venezuela. The State Department gets the right to buy 20% of NABEP's oil at cost, and preferential access to the remaining 80% of output.

The deal marks ‌a striking change of fortune for Betancourt, who four people familiar with U.S. policy in Venezuela said was key to U.S. strategy and planning in the lead-up to the January 3 operation that removed former President Maduro from power and flew him to New York to face charges of drug-trafficking, which Maduro denies.

Asked about the investigations of Betancourt, a U.S. official who declined to be named ​said most of the legal challenges were nearly a decade old — and that he currently has no legal problems in the United States. NABEP's record of pumping oil in Venezuela made Betancourt the best partner to help boost output under the arrangement, the official said.

Sarah Chouraqui, NABEP's lawyer, said Betancourt had a strong record of operating in complex energy markets. "The allegations in question have been examined extensively by authorities in multiple jurisdictions, and no charges have been brought against him," she said in an email.

Chouraqui did not address questions about his assistance to the Trump administration or his legal cases.

INFORMATION THAT HELPED ENFORCE U.S. BLOCKADE

In the months before Maduro's capture, the billionaire provided information that helped enforce a U.S. naval blockade targeting sanctioned oil tankers operating in Venezuela, which led to the seizure or interdiction of more than a dozen vessels, according to the four people who spoke on ‌condition of anonymity. He also facilitated negotiations with officials including Delcy Rodriguez, who became interim president after Maduro's capture.

The ⁠Venezuelan government did not respond to requests for comment.

After Maduro's removal, Betancourt's role as a key intermediary continued, helping broker oil deals and other partnerships and continuing to assist communications between Washington and Caracas to kickstart Venezuela's economy, according to seven sources.

In January, Betancourt helped broker a key oil trading agreement that has led to the export of more than 135 million barrels of crude and fuel to the United States, Europe, India and the Caribbean so far, according to vessel monitoring data and ⁠six people with knowledge of the negotiations. That's about half of all oil exports through the end of August.

Betancourt has also popped in on meetings at Venezuela's Miraflores presidential palace, according to two people familiar with the matter. He was also at Miraflores during this week's visit by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Wright told reporters, though Betancourt did not appear with Wright and Rodriguez at a signing ceremony for oil deals.

Betancourt has been investigated in the United States, Spain and Switzerland but never indicted.

Earlier this year U.S. federal prosecutors in Florida paused their investigation into Betancourt in connection with an alleged plan that involved embezzling over $1 billion from Venezuela's state-owned oil company ​and ​laundering it through real estate in Miami and bank accounts in Malta and Switzerland.

Two of those people said U.S. prosecutors had been subsequently discouraged by supervisors from investigating Betancourt further.

Prosecutors ​on the case were not given a rationale, four people familiar with the case said.

After the investigation stalled, U.S. officials ‌pressured the Swiss government to ease its inquiries into the tycoon, said four people familiar with the matter. Switzerland, which was also investigating Betancourt for money-laundering, dropped its request to extradite him from the United Kingdom in May, said the sources.

The Zurich Public Prosecutor's Office declined to comment on whether the United States influenced the decision to withdraw its extradition request, but said the case against Betancourt was still proceeding.

"The extradition request was withdrawn because of particular aspects of UK extradition law, which we cannot discuss in detail," the Office said. "This step concerns only the extradition proceedings in the UK. The criminal proceedings against the accused are otherwise unaffected and will continue."

The withdrawal was unusual, said Mark Pieth, a Swiss legal scholar and anti-corruption expert. "You would not do that if the case is continuing," he said.

The United Kingdom's Home Office declined to comment.

A YOUNG GENERATION OF BUSINESS LEADERS

Betancourt is a prominent member of the so-called Bolichicos — a younger generation of business people who amassed fortunes during the administration of former Venezuelan leader Hugo Chavez. His company Derwick Associates won roughly $2 billion in government contracts to build power plants during the country's electricity crisis in the 2010s — some without competitive bidding — despite having little construction experience.

Government data later showed many of the plants operated at a fraction of their intended capacity or not ‌at all, as Venezuela's power grid continued to suffer widespread blackouts. Betancourt and Derwick have repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said the facilities were completed and that later failures resulted from ​mismanagement by state authorities. Rodriguez told a press conference on Wednesday that all legal proceedings against Betancourt's companies in Venezuela were dismissed years ago.

In 2012, Betancourt entered into a partnership with state-controlled ​company PDVSA to operate mature fields in western Venezuela. These would eventually become the core production of NABEP, which Betancourt co-founded with Florida billionaire Harry ​Sargeant in April 2024. Sargeant sold his shares in NABEP last month.

Mauricio Claver-Carone, a Miami businessman and former Trump administration adviser who implemented U.S. policy in Caracas in an unofficial role, told Reuters last month that Betancourt is a useful intermediary between the ‌Trump administration and Rodriguez because he understands the oil business in both countries. He added that Betancourt had been ​helpful to the first Trump administration.

But several former U.S. intelligence officials, prosecutors and diplomats ​privately expressed concern regarding Betancourt's influence on U.S. policy, because of the previous investigation in the U.S. and ongoing investigation in Switzerland, as well as his proximity to high-ranking officials from the former Hugo Chavez and Maduro governments.

Federal prosecutors are "scratching their heads," said one former prosecutor with knowledge of the situation.

Before the Miami-based investigation into Betancourt was put on hold, six sources said he had been identified as an unnamed unindicted co-conspirator in an alleged plan by former Venezuelan energy officials and their associates to launder more than $1 billion misappropriated from the state-owned PDVSA oil company. Ten people have ​been indicted since 2018.

In Spain, authorities launched a new investigation into Betancourt for money laundering last year involving $4 billion ‌allegedly embezzled from PDVSA, according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.

Spain's National Court and the Venezuelan state oil company did not respond to requests for comment.

Once he was free to leave the UK, Betancourt traveled to Venezuela in ​late June and again in July, both times departing from West Palm Beach, Florida, according to flight manifests seen by Reuters.

Betancourt's lawyer Chouraqui did not comment on his travel.

title: Judge reinforces order halting immediate work on Trump’s 250-foot arch
description: A judge ordered the Trump administration to provide 48 hours’ notice before construction begins on the site of President Donald Trump’s planned arch.
fullText:
A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Friday, Sept. 4, to provide 48 hours' notice before moving forward with work on the site of a planned 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that the administration must inform the court "before engaging in any activity on Memorial Circle other than on-site information gathering" to identify underground cultural artifacts.

Chutkan reinforced her order a day after Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum announced plans on Sept. 3 to break ground at the site of the arch in the coming days.

"We are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck, at Memorial Circle on Columbia Island between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery," Burgum wrote on X. "This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World."

The proposed arch, one of several projects Trump has launched in an effort to change the landscape of the nation's capital, has been controversial from the start. A group of three veterans and a historian filed a lawsuit in February to oppose the project.

The plaintiffs asked Chutkan on Sept. 4 to issue a 14-day restraining order to block the Trump administration from "taking any steps to construct or to direct or facilitate construction of any structure in Memorial Circle."

Despite Burgum's announcement, the government argued in a court filing that the planned activity at the site of the proposed arch is standard archaeological survey work. The administration intends to mechanically excavate four test pits no earlier than Sept. 21 and the land is expected to be restored by Oct. 31, per the filing.

"This activity is not construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, of an arch," the government said.

The proposed arch is also awaiting final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, which would need to grant an exception to a 130-foot building height limit.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Judge reinforces order halting immediate work on Trump's 250-foot arch

title: Trump’s ‘Catch-Me-If-You-Can’ presidency keeps finding ways around the law
description: A plain reading of the law about presidents on coins says the face of a living president should not be on currency. And yet President Donald Trump’s is, after his Treasury Department exploited a diffe...
fullText:
A plain reading of the law about presidents on coins says the face of a living president should not be on currency. And yet President Donald Trump's is, after his Treasury Department exploited a different law related to commemorative coins.

The law says a president must not commit the US military into hostilities for longer than 60 days without congressional approval. The US has been in a conflict with Iran for more than six months, although the administration says it has taken time-outs in the war. Previous presidents from both parties have danced around this requirement, but nothing on the level of Trump's war on Iran.

Chief Justice John Roberts called it "likely unlawful" for Trump to tear down part of the White House and build something else. And yet construction is happening around the clock to get that White House ballroom done for Trump to enjoy.

Laws would seem to require Congress to approve the construction of a triumphal arch adjacent to Arlington National Cemetery. The administration isn't waiting and the Department of Interior appears primed to start excavation shortly.

The law says suspected criminals should not be put to death without a trial. And yet the US military has taken out numerous alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific.

The law says Congress creates agencies of the federal government, like USAID, the US Department of Education and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Trump has tried to end some of them anyway, either through starvation or outright deletion.

The law says Congress decides where money should go. That didn't stop Trump's administration from cutting research funding and aid money it simply disagreed with.

The law says the government should not be entering people's homes without a judicial warrant. But Immigration and Customs Enforcement has utilized that power.

The law says the Federal Reserve should operate independently, but that isn't stopping Trump from trying to pressure the Fed to lower interest rates — most recently via a threat to cease trade with top partners.

The list goes on, and with it the complicated legal arguments the Trump administration has made – in those instances when it has had to make them.

Even when faced with setbacks in court, Trump's administration has brazenly looked for end-runs.

A judge ruled Trump's administration can't ignore the law and put his name alongside John F. Kennedy's on the Kennedy Center. But the administration plans to add it to the building anyway, by adding an inscription giving Trump credit for the rehab job. And if the administration can't put the name on the building, it threatens to tear the whole thing down.

The tearing-down of buildings the president should not be able to tear down is an apt analogy for this whole presidency. Once something is gone, it's gone. It doesn't matter if getting rid of it was illegal.

Roberts sided with liberals on the court to argue – in an unsuccessful dissent – that Trump's East Wing project should be halted because it was "likely unlawful." In his dissent, Roberts quoted Winston Churchill during World War II.

"We shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us," Churchill had said. Roberts didn't mention that Churchill made those comments to argue the British House of Commons should be rebuilt as it had stood before it was destroyed by Nazi bombs. Churchill wanted to rebuild it as a monument to the British form of government.

Trump saw the White House East Wing as a tear-down project — a (likely) illegal tear-down in Roberts' eyes. But Trump's monument to himself – one of many — is getting built nonetheless. Asking Congress for the taxpayer money to help with the project came only after the walls were torn down.

It has become a pattern during Trump's second term that the president does something; Congress shrugs; and the Supreme Court allows him to proceed, regardless of whether what he's doing is, strictly speaking, legal.

A week before Roberts' historical lament, the liberal Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson blasted the court's conservatives, including Roberts, for allowing Trump's executive order meant to cut down on mail-in voting to proceed, again on a technicality.

The White House has a "Catch-Me-If-You-Can approach," Jackson said.

In the case of disrupting mail-in ballots, Trump may ultimately get caught; the executive order still faces lawsuits and a new injunction that make it seem impossible to impose, at least for this election.

Trump also got caught on birthright citizenship, where justices rejected his attempt to set aside the Constitution's 14th Amendment. And on tariffs, they said no, he could not exploit national emergency laws to upend the economy.

He's still looking for ways around that decision.

But on so many other issues, Trump's administration has picked the laws it wants to follow, diverted funds here or there, and said little in public about what it's up to. Congress has shrugged. Courts have had trouble keeping up, and the Supreme Court has preferred to let Trump go about his business while things get sorted out.

That dynamic seems likely to change, at least somewhat, come next year if Democrats win control of either the House or the Senate. They will try to restrict funding for Trump's goals.

But it will be an interesting question for Democrats who want to replace Trump in the White House in 2029. Should they spend even more taxpayer money to tear down the East Wing behemoth he's building? They won't be able to go back and take the coins with his face out of circulation. They can't un-deport people who didn't get a hearing. And it will take time and effort, if the next president is so inclined, to rebuild the system of scientific and medical research funding the Trump administration cut back.

On so many of the things Trump has done, catching up may not even be an option.

title: Ty Cobb on midterms: Trump intends ‘to steal these elections where possible’
description: Former Trump White House lawyer Ty Cobb said Thursday that President Trump would attempt to “steal” the 2026 midterm elections “where possible.” Cobb, in an appearance on MS NOW, discussed reports of ...
fullText:
Former Trump White House lawyer Ty Cobb said Thursday that President Trump would attempt to "steal" the 2026 midterm elections "where possible."

Cobb, in an appearance on MS NOW, discussed reports of GOP lawmakers declining to attend a Republican National Committee event, underlining concerns about Trump's political brand almost two years into his second term.

A source familiar told The Hill that the National Republican Congressional Committee distributed more than 2,000 tickets for the convention and that around 100 members and candidates were confirmed to attend. Lawmakers are expected to contribute a minimum of $25,000 to take part.

"Well, I think the Republicans who are saying no are being strategic," Cobb said. "But at the same time, he's [Trump] sitting on $400 million in campaign money that he could donate to some of these elections. And he's not."

Cobb added that, "It also plays into a narrative that I think people are undervaluing, which is I think Trump doesn't feel he needs to spend this money because it is his intention to interfere with the elections and to steal these elections where possible."

He raised the possibility that Trump could "urge" House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to refuse to swear in Democratic candidates following the midterm elections. Johnson was an active backer of Trump's efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss to former President Biden.

The Trump administration is still pushing to restrict mail-in voting for the midterms, even as states start sending out early ballots. The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to allow for the U.S. Postal Service's implementation of Trump's executive order targeting mail voting.

The Postal Service's plan would mandate that states' mail-in ballots meet design requirements — such as unique barcodes and an official logo — and require election officials to upload lists of voters who are eligible to vote by mail. If a ballot doesn't meet the specifications or someone is not on the submitted list, the service would refuse to deliver it.

In a July appearance on MS NOW, Cobb argued that moves from Trump like this are rooted in his refusal to accept his 2020 defeat.

"The most grievous thing that ever happened to him was he lost an election," he said at the time. "As a malignant narcissist, he just can't abide that."

title: Trump says ‘nobody will’ build monuments for him once he’s gone
description: President Donald Trump did not dispute that he is building monuments to himself amid his architectural blitz in Washington, DC, saying in a recent interview that “nobody will do it once I’m gone.”
fullText:
President Donald Trump did not dispute that he is building monuments to himself amid his architectural blitz in Washington, DC, saying in a recent interview that "nobody will do it once I'm gone."

When asked about the monuments, such as the "triumphal arch," by New York Magazine, Trump agreed that he was building them for himself.

"That's true," Trump said. "Nobody will do it once I'm gone. When I leave here, nobody will."

The president has been intensely focused on construction of a White House ballroom and other projects in his second term, much to the chagrin of some congressional Republicans and Trump advisers, some of whom told New York Magazine that harping on the ballroom could harm the GOP's midterm election chances and make staying on message more difficult.

Trump told the magazine, however, that "the people should be thankful" for the ballroom.

"A lot of people said, 'Don't do this interview.' But I'm proud of the work I'm doing," the president said.

Trump has argued that the ballroom is necessary for national security, emphasizing plans for a drone port on the roof and an underground bunker, as well as bulletproof windows. Meanwhile, the administration is set to break ground on the 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery in the next two weeks.

But ultimately, as sources told CNN earlier this year, it all comes down to the president's legacy.

"Look at Donald Trump's life, look at what he's done: Built things that no one will ever tear down," a source close to him told CNN in May, noting that even if successors undo his policies, the ballroom will likely still stand.

"The one thing they can't tear down will be the East Wing. That is his lasting impact. That's why he cares so deeply: legacy sh*t," the source said.

title: 24 hours that show how preoccupied Trump is
description: It can be difficult to decide which Roman metaphor more aptly captures President Donald Trump’s posture these days.
fullText:
It can be difficult to decide which Roman metaphor more aptly captures President Donald Trump's posture these days.

Is it "bread and circuses," feeding the American people a series of distractions — amusing or otherwise — from their worries about the economy? Or is it Nero, fiddling with his ballroom plans while the Republican Party's midterm hopes burn?

What's clear is that Trump and his administration aren't going to course correct any time soon.

The last 24 hours have been a case in point. And the last couple weeks have been inauspicious for anyone who hoped Trump might suddenly focus on the political task at hand.

Thursday marked exactly two months until Election Day 2026. And the first votes are about to be cast, with North Carolina sending out mail ballots on Friday.

But despite a bevy of polling showing Americans want Trump to focus on affordability and the economy, he appears preoccupied with anything but.

On Thursday alone, we learned the Trump administration has hired a new pool contractor to clean up the mess he made of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, announced the start of construction on Trump's 250-foot "triumphal arch" and launched a series of arcade-style video games, including one that allows users to arrest undocumented immigrants.

The White House is also reportedly launching a reality show-like competition for entrepreneurs, just weeks after Trump's "Patriot Games" flopped and after an actual reality show from the Department of Transportation was released. (It says a nonprofit paid for it; not taxpayers.)

Trump even sat for an interview — and gave a construction tour, of course — for the New York Magazine piece.

Reporter Ben Terris reported that the president's official calendar is "peppered with meetings about other projects around Washington that can often last an hour or longer."

And in perhaps the most eyebrow-raising scene, Trump actually agrees with Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's contention that he's building monuments to himself because he doesn't think others can be counted on to do it.

"That's true," Trump said. "Nobody will do it once I'm gone. When I leave here, nobody will."

The fact that Trump would say this out loud is stunning. Ossoff meant this as a dig.

But it also suggests Trump might be feeling the pressure to get these projects done fast. He has a finite amount of time to plaster his name on things and build things that he'll be remembered by. It could get more difficult by January, when Democrats could control one or both chambers of Congress.

Trump even talks about how it will supposedly be impossible for Democrats to demolish his ballroom, if they wanted to. ("It's nuclear concrete," he told New York Magazine. "I think it would be very hard. It's meant for if there's a nuclear attack.")

Terris also runs through how Trump in his public appearances often seems distracted by his construction projects as he's attending to much more serious business.

And that's really the problem with all of this, at least if you're a congressional Republican staring at a concerning midterm election.

It's not just that Trump is distracted; it's that he's focused on things that polls show Americans view as frivolous and don't want — at the expense of things they really want him to do (i.e. lowering prices and ending the war with Iran).

Trump's ballroom is 2-to-1 unpopular.

Americans opposed his 250-foot "triumphal arch" 52%-21% in an April poll.

A July poll showed 65% of Americans described themselves as upset or dissatisfied with the ballroom, arch and Reflecting Pool projects.

While Trump tries to put his name on things like the Kennedy Center, just 9% of Americans think that's appropriate for him to do as an incumbent president.

And Trump's other preoccupation in recent days and weeks — his new trade war with Canada, which led him move to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America" — fares little better. Reuters-Ipsos polling this week showed Americans opposed the Canada tariffs 57%-20% and the "Lake America" renaming 63%-14%.

Trump last week held a White House event for the latter move, which it turns out even his fellow Republicans oppose by double digits.

All of this cements a tough picture for the GOP. Polling has for months shown that Americans view Trump as neglecting more important fare.

CBS News polling has recently shown 78% of Americans said he's not focused enough on lowering prices, and July CNN polling shows around the same percentage (73%) said he hasn't paid enough attention to the country's most important problems.

It's not fair to say Trump has completely neglected the cost of living.

He recently announced he would pause tariffs on imported beef to try to lower prices for consumers, and on Friday he threatened to stop trading with other countries if the Federal Reserve doesn't lower interest rates.

Both moves could theoretically save people money.

But both moves also betray Trump's preference for questionable quick fixes. The beef tariffs move, for example, is expected to have a negligible impact, CNN reported, while irritating domestic cattle ranchers and even some Republicans. And the extortionate threat to the Fed seems unlikely to bear fruit. (Indeed, lowering interest rates could actually send inflation higher.)

The CNN poll in July contained another telling finding. Fully 66% of Americans said Trump did not put the good of the country above his own personal gain. That included 76% of independents and 30% of Republicans.

And more than a month later, with the 2026 general election truly kicking off, it's as if he's bent on proving those people right.

title: Pelosi, Omar join Trump and Schiff as unlikely alliance pushes to onshore key industry
description: Adam Schiff, Nancy Pelosi and Ilhan Omar back Donald Trump's federal film tax incentive to bring movie production back to California and America.
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE: President Donald Trump has gained several unlikely allies, including the man who led his first impeachment trial, in a major push to bring motion picture production back to California from other countries.

Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., who represented studio-heavy Burbank in Congress, was joined by Reps. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., in echoing support for Trump's federal tax incentive plan to draw major film projects back to where it began.

"We've been promoting that for a long time. I'm glad he finally arrived at it," Pelosi told Fox News Digital when asked about the plan on the Capitol grounds.

Paramount Escalates Threat To Leave California As Dem Ag's Antitrust Lawsuit Stalls Warner Bros Merger

Schiff tweeted earlier this week that he is "in strong agreement with the president."

The Democrat, who has accused Trump of colluding with Moscow to win the election and whom the president has responded to by calling him "pencil-neck," said it is time for Republicans and Democrats to "work together… get this done and bring the movie magic back to America."

Schiff Attack On Trump's Dc Indycar Race Backfires After Driver Points Out Contradiction

"Congress should immediately take up and pass a federal film tax incentive to bring back these good-paying jobs that we've lost to other countries."

Omar told Fox News Digital a similar refrain, adding that she has worked separately to attract film projects to Minneapolis.

Film Producer Says 'Made In America' Movies Can Help Revive Hollywood's Struggling Industry

She referenced "Fargo," the 1996 Coen Brothers comedy starring William H. Macy as an example of Minnesota's ability to host large projects. The "Mighty Ducks" series starring Emilio Estevez and Joshua Jackson also filmed heavily in the Twin Cities during its 1990s run.

"When I was in the Minnesota House, I was very supportive of Minnesota having subsidies so we can have more movies being made inside Minnesota like the movie 'Fargo'," she said.

She said the end of subsidies from St. Paul recently "made it less fun trying to run into people who were actually doing the production."

"It could be a really cool thing [and] also bring us money to states that can use it."

Trump appointed legendary actors Jon Voight, Mel Gibson and Sylvester Stallone special envoys to Hollywood. Gibson previously told Fox News that for a recent film, it was cheaper to fly the entire crew to Europe for three days than to shoot for one day in Los Angeles.

"There's something really wrong there," he said, adding that another actor, ex-California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, tried to assuage the problem while in office but was met with "obstacles."

Last year, another Trump foil also got on board with the idea of Washington bolstering Hollywood.

"California built the film industry – and we're ready to bring even more jobs home… Now it's time for a real federal partnership to Make America Film Again," said California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson contributed to this report.

title: Trump thrashes Zhao to reach last four of British Open
description: Judd Trump thrashes world number one Zhao Xintong 5-1 as he moves into the semi-finals of the British Open.
fullText:
Judd Trump thrashed world number one Zhao Xintong 5-1 as he moved into the semi-finals of the British Open.

The Englishman will now face Aaron Hill or Jak Jones on Saturday, with Mark Selby taking on Liam Highfield in the other last-four encounter.

"When it goes down to two or one table it is a completely different set-up and you feel like the tournament comes alive," Trump said on Channel 5.

Earlier on Friday, Highfield had defeated teenage star Stan Moody 5-2, while Selby claimed a thumping 5-0 victory over Jack Lisowski.

And Trump delivered more of the same in the evening against the man who recently deposed him at the top of the rankings.

The 37-year-old, who has won 31 ranking titles, opened with a break of 101 and 57 to take the opening two frames before Zhao responded with a century of his own.

However, Trump restricted his Chinese opponent to just 29 points over the following three frames, while knocking in two further half-centuries to easily advance.

"[I was] probably a little more determined than normal," Trump added.

"In the past when I have lost the number one spot or people put other players as the favourite, you don't have that as number one and have that same demeanour of wanting to prove everyone wrong or that I'm the best."

title: US issues sanctions on Turkish bank that it calls a 'critical financial lifeline' for Iran
description: The Trump administration announced Friday that it has imposed sanctions on a Turkish financial institution as part of its latest effort to sever “critical financial lifelines” for the Iranian governme...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration announced Friday that it has imposed sanctions on a Turkish financial institution as part of its latest effort to sever "critical financial lifelines" for the Iranian government.

The actions against Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi Anonim Sirketi come after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week launched "Operation Economic Outcast, " Washington's new effort to isolate already heavily sanctioned Iran from its remaining trading partners to try to get it to capitulate to U.S. demands after more than six months of war.

The Treasury Department accused the Turkish bank and its entities of being established to enable Iran's efforts to transfer oil revenues from China to Turkey, where they could then be converted to cash and gold. It also said the institution "knowingly offered" banking services to Iranian financial entities, including those already sanctioned by the U.S. government in 2022 for funneling Tehran's oil sales.

Bessent, who had told The Associated Press earlier this week that another bank would face economic penalties, said financial institutions with ties to Iran will "continue to find out the hard way that we are serious about Operation Economic Outcast."

"While we hope no more banks will need to be sanctioned, that ultimately depends on how quickly the international community comes to its senses and ceases support of the murderous Iranian regime," he said in a press release Friday. "We know who you are, we know where you are, and we will continue to take action together with our allies and partners until we have buried the head of the Iranian snake."

But so far, the goal to force those that still do business with Iran to cut off financial ties or face U.S. retaliation has fallen flat, with promises of an "economic D-Day" for a group of countries that could include China and India quickly turning into warnings and negotiations with Iran's trading partners.

Bessent had previously told reporters that he wanted countries to have an opportunity to shift away from Iran before it was too late in a bid to avoid upending the global financial system.

The Trump administration's reluctance to penalize major trading partners that still do business with Iran was on display last week when the U.S. took steps to limit an Egyptian bank's operations in the United Arab Emirates but stopped short of imposing sanctions.

The U.S. also has resumed military strikes in recent days, prompting Iranian retaliation in the region. It's unclear what the outcome of the two-pronged strategy will be for President Donald Trump, who has struggled to end an unpopular war with an intransigent Iranian government as energy prices rise and pose problems for Republicans before November's midterm congressional elections.

Targeted in the latest U.S. sanctions is Golden Global Investment Bank, which was founded in 2019 as Turkey's first investment bank to offer "banking services and alternative financing methods" to foreign companies, according to its website.

The Istanbul-based bank, which is largely unfamiliar to most Turks, says it aims to increase Turkey's foreign trade through target markets in neighboring countries.

The Treasury announcement came a day after Turkey's state-run Halkbank declared it had reached a settlement with the U.S. Justice Department in a nine-year case focused on violating sanctions with Iran.

In that case, senior officials at Halkbank were said to have illegally moved about $20 billion worth of Iranian oil revenues. U.S. prosecutors claimed high-ranking Turkish government officials received millions of dollars in bribes to protect the scheme.

The Halkbank case caused a rift in U.S.-Turkey relations, with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan personally lobbying the White House to have the case dropped.

title: Trump administration warms to Zambia despite crackdown worries
description: Washington Democrats said they’re alarmed about post-election violence.
fullText:
The Trump administration is warming to Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema following his disputed reelection despite growing concerns in Washington about a post-election crackdown.

US Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia attended Hichilema's inauguration this week during his second trip to the continent in the role. He also met separately with the Zambian leader. Hichilema said Zambia looks "forward to further strengthening our bilateral relations" with the US.

A State Department spokesperson told Semafor that the trip was a continuation of a decades-old relationship. "After 62 years of diplomatic relations, the United States remains committed to Zambia's success. We look forward to working with Zambia's government, private sector, and people to deepen a partnership that delivers tangible and enduring benefits for both countries," the spokesperson said.

The Trump administration's posture towards the government in Lusaka contrasts with warnings from Democrats on Capitol Hill, some of whom had urged the State Department before the August 13 vote to press for a free and fair election.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told Semafor that "democratic backsliding in Zambia is a major concern for the Southern African region," adding that post-election "violence and arbitrary arrest" are signs of "a clear divergence from Zambia's legacy of competitive elections and peaceful transfers of power." She called on Hichilema and his party to move forward with reforms because "clear violations of democratic gains threaten not only the safety and security of Zambians but also the positive relationship the US has built with the Hichilema administration."

Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio to "call on President Hichilema to release the electoral results from Zambia's polling stations, investigate the fatal shooting of former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya, and allow the courts to hear legal challenges." He cited the need for a "firm response" ahead of upcoming elections in Angola, Kenya, and Nigeria. Kafwaya was killed during a police raid on a house occupied by opposition leaders following the August election.

Senate Africa subcommittee ranking member Cory Booker, D-N.J., called the killing of Kafwaya and the arrests of opposition members "deeply concerning."

A representative for Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jim Risch, R-Idaho, declined to comment. Other Republican lawmakers working on Africa policy did not return requests for comment by press time.

Zambia's election commission declared Hichilema the winner on August 18 with about 60% of the vote against opposition candidate Brian Mundubile's roughly 38%. Mundubile has alleged irregularities and election observers have also reported inflated vote tallies and improper administration. Authorities sealed off the courts on the final day to file an election petition, clearing the way for Hichilema's inauguration.

Post-election crackdowns left Mundubile and many of his allies facing treason charges that a UN human rights official called "concocted."

Zambia is central to the US-backed Lobito Corridor linking Angola, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Zambia's copper belt to the Atlantic. But ties between the US and Zambia frayed this year following reports the State Department was tying health funding to preferential mineral access for US firms, a plan that Zambia rejected.

title: Trump says Iran conflict, which has killed 18 US service members and injured hundreds more, is ‘small potatoes’
description: President Donald Trump on Friday labeled the Iran war “small potatoes,” the latest attempt to minimize a six-month conflict that caused a spike in gas prices and led to the deaths of 18 American servi...
fullText:
President Donald Trump on Friday labeled the Iran war "small potatoes," the latest attempt to minimize a six-month conflict that caused a spike in gas prices and led to the deaths of 18 American service-members.

"A lot of people don't call it a war. I call it a military conflict because it's small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing," he said in the Oval Office.

A day earlier, Vice President JD Vance said the conflict shouldn't be termed a "war" since major combat operations ended months ago.

Trump similarly cast the conflict as periodic and low-grade, despite routine rounds of back-and-forth strikes.

"I would say that it's intermittent. You know, we do intermittent strikes," Trump said, adding: "There's a lot of truth that we're not fighting right now. There's no fighting."

This week the US said it had targeted nearly 60 military targets around the Strait of Hormuz — including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites — while simultaneously escorting ships through the waterway.

The administration had signaled it was moving past a military strategy, focusing instead on choking off Iran financially by applying sanctions on its trading partners. So far, however, the US has stopped short of punishing China, Tehran's biggest economic lifeline.

Trump, who plans to host Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit this month, downplayed the assistance Beijing was providing.

"They are not really involved. Very little involvement by China. China could have plenty of involvement," he said.

He also extolled potential new routes and pipelines that could bypass the Strait of Hormuz, including an overland alternative through Syria.

"They're going to end up with a horrible strait that's not really necessary any more," he said.

Trump also raised the prospect of a new operation soon to take out a suspected Iranian nuclear site south of Tehran.

"We may hit Pickaxe very soon," he said, referring to the underground facility where Iran is believed to have moved some of its stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

But he still insisted the conflict was not a war.

"It's a military conflict, but it's very intermittent. I could see somebody not calling it a war," he said.

He continued: "I don't think it matters what you call it. What matters is the fact that we have had tremendous success."

This story has been updated with additional details.

title: Ken Paxton responds after Trump says his suit doesn't 'look so great'
description: Paxton brushed off Trump’s wardrobe critique during a Sept. 3 appearance on Fox News, saying Texas is “a relatively casual place.”
fullText:
Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton is reacting to President Donald Trump's criticism of the way he dresses.

Paxton brushed off Trump's wardrobe critique during a Sept. 3 appearance on Fox News, saying Texas is "a relatively casual place" and pointing to the Lone Star State's summer heat.

"I've got my sports jacket on. I love it. Texas is a relatively casual place in the summer, and it's hot. We adjust. We wear cowboy boots, and we wear a blazer, and we're all good," Paxton said.

Ken Paxton responds to Trump trashing his clothes: I've got my sports jacket on, I love it. Texas is a rather casual place in the summer and it's hot. We adjust. Wear cowboy boots, a blazer, and we're good. pic.twitter.com/9uaVglIOGF

— Acyn (@Acyn) September 3, 2026

Trump criticized Paxton's appearance during a Rose Garden dinner at the White House on Sept. 2, while also praising his record as Texas attorney general.

"And I say this, it's so insulting to him, but I might as well say it. You might not like the way he looks, you might not love his look, you might not love his television interviews, but he was the best attorney general in the country, perhaps," Trump said.

Trump continued, saying Paxton's record "speaks a lot louder than the suit he's wearing that doesn't look so great."

Trump also targeted Paxton's Democratic opponent, James Talarico, claiming Talarico eats meat and later becomes sick.

"Now he says he loves meat," Trump said, before claiming Talarico eats meat and then "throws up all over the place."

Trump added: "In Texas, if you don't eat meat, you're in deep trouble."

Trump's comments about Talarico's food habits aren't the first — in May, Trump accused him of being a vegan, something Talarico denies.

fullText:
A string of distractions on the US government’s own website invite you to catch pixelated migrants – showing gaming’s potential to be nastily weaponised

The Trump White House on Thursday released a horrible little propaganda arcade via its website, a collection of nasty riffs on popular games. Wrapped in the cutesy, nostalgic aesthetic of early-90s pixel art, these mindless fascist diversions are harmless-looking, but their intent is stomach-turning: this is the appropriation of play in service of propaganda. It’s just the latest in a series of attempts from Trump’s administration to use video game memes and imagery to further its messaging.

Having riffed on Halo and Pokémon in social media ads last year, inviting potential ICE recruits to “stop the flood” and “catch ’em all”, this time the administration has ripped off a series of recognisable games. Flappy Bill, perhaps the least gross, is a version of the old mobile hit Flappy Bird, except here you’re an eagle with a scroll in its claws. Supply Line could almost be an educational game about healthy food in schools, where you sort junk food off a conveyor belt destined for school lunches, except for some reason you play as a boxer who becomes more bloodied with every seed-oil containing, ultra-processed food item that you fail to punch into the garbage chute.

Then come the really nasty ones: Build the Wall, which warps Tetris into a game where you must fortify the southern border to keep out “the coming horde”, and an evil little take on Snake where you patrol the Rio Grande, collecting brown people who then follow you around in orange jumpsuits. The final game is Trump Savings Tycoon, where you “fill your kids’ Trump accounts” by catching bills and gold coins in a net. (The algae-beset Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is depicted in the foreground, inaccurately coloured in blue.)

I have played all of them, so that you don’t have to. Build the Wall and Rio Run are actively disgusting, built around the naked dehumanisation of migrants, but mostly these games are just embarrassing. Like most things that come from the Trump White House communications team, they are mean-spirited, unimaginative and lazy. I have a strong suspicion that they are vibe-coded using AI, and I almost hope that they are, because the idea of humans spending their precious time on Earth making these horrid, half-arsed games makes me even sadder than playing them did.

Anyone involved in the creation of the original games that the White House Arcade is ripping off is surely cringeing. Members of the original Halo team were moved to speak out on social media after the White House posted a picture of Trump as Master Chief last year; I wonder if Sega will have anything to say about this trailer, which opens with a digital chorus singing “Magaaaa”, soundtracking the sorry collection with music that sounds a lot like Sonic’s Green Hill Zone.

The leveraging of video games and their imagery for political influence has been under way for some time, beginning perhaps with 2014’s Gamergate, an online harassment movement that was stoked by Steve Bannon and far-right website Breitbart. Trump, alongside other rightwing regimes, has had an enormous head start on this front. “The use of video game content, culture and aesthetics for communication is a feature of Trump’s White House, rather than a bug, because much of the modern political right emerged from toxic game communities,” says George Osborn, author of Power Play: Video Games, Politics and the Battle for Global Influence.

“Activists who shaped the Gamergate movement have become an established part of the political right … Until now, it seemed to be restricted to social media posting. I estimated that video game-coded posts had approximately twice the reach of a regular White House Instagram post, suggesting it was able to simultaneously rile up audiences offended by its post and delight supporters. But the deployment of an arcade on its website marks a change of course … Now, it appears that Trump’s White House is ready to use games to begin to try to win over audiences – escalating from appropriating video game culture to ensnaring the medium itself for its own ends.”

Artists and activists have been using video games to put across political messages for a very long time. I have played games about escaping war-torn countries; about examining the paperwork of desperate people at the border of a fictional eastern bloc country; about running a dictatorship or taking one down. Governments, however, are new players in this space.

These games, in line with the Trump administration’s wider social media and communications strategy, are culture-war shitposting. They are almost entirely valueless, and exist more to rile us up than to actually persuade anyone of anything. If we attach too much outrage to them, we are being drawn into someone else’s game; it is deeply unlikely that a round of Rio Run is about to radicalise anyone who isn’t already fully on board with Trump’s whole schtick. But at a time when the Saudi Arabian wealth fund now co-owns one of the world’s biggest game publishers alongside an investment firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, gaming’s propagandist potential should not be a blind spot.

The Shadowy Powers that Trump Could Use to End American Democracy
description: Sasha...
fullText:
Two Washington insiders are sounding the alarm about what could happen if Trump activates the top-secret Presidential Emergency Action Documents.

In early 2024, as the presidential election season heated up and Donald Trump’s antidemocratic language intensified, two alumni of the Washington power structure began publishing a series of memos titled “Dancing in the Dark” in The Washington Spectator.

The authors were Mark Medish, an attorney who served as a special assistant to the president, a senior director at the National Security Council, and a deputy assistant to the secretary of the US Treasury under President Bill Clinton; and Joel McCleary, who was a deputy assistant to the president during the Carter administration.

In the lead-up to the 2024 election, Medish and McCleary published three long essays detailing ways in which Trump and the MAGA movement were corroding democratic norms. Then they went quiet. Two weeks ago, the duo re-emerged with an alarming new essay, “It’s the Power, Stupid: Dancing in the Dark, Part 4.”

The warnings in Medish and McCleary’s latest essay are stark. They center around the possibility that a cornered, wrathful Trump—enabled by supine leadership in the Justice Department, the Pentagon, and other key departments of government, as well as by GOP leadership in Congress—could declare a national emergency in the run-up to and aftermath of the midterm elections. Their fear is that, if he does so, he might then activate the highly secretive, Cold War era Presidential Emergency Action Documents (PEADs), authored to ensure continuity of the government following a nuclear attack, in an attempt to suspend the constitutional order.

PEADs exist outside of the regular legislative and legal framework of the country. Drafted by a series of White House lawyers from the Eisenhower presidency onward, they are, by definition, extra-constitutional. Congress isn’t looped in on their specifics; few attorneys within government, outside of a handful at the epicenter of White House power, are thought to have seen them; only a select few cabinet members, including the vice president, the defense secretary, the national security director, and the head of the CIA, are thought to have access to them; and those who do are forbidden to even acknowledge their existence. “They’re in a weird category of executive legal authority,” Medish told me. “The way to think about this is a set of contingency plans, in effect draft orders based on contingency scenarios—what should the president do in order to maintain continuity of government?”

Over the past several decades, according to those who have studied this shadowy world, the Department of Defense has spent billions of dollars out of secret, black-budget funds, building up an infrastructure to implement PEADs and other continuity-of-government measures should an emergency situation arise. Much of this was done, McCleary alleges, at the direction of Dick Cheney and Donald Rumsfeld during the War on Terror, although the mechanisms for mass incarceration of political dissidents were worked out earlier, especially during the Reagan administration, under an operational plan known as Rex 84, when national-security officials strategized how to respond should there be a mass uprising against US interventions in Latin America. Today, under the National Security Presidential Memorandum-7 (NSPM-7) directive, the FBI and other agencies, in conjunction with Big Tech and other purveyors of surveillance infrastructure, are investigating large numbers of political dissidents and critics.

“There’s a pretty firm belief that detention is strongly in these PEADs,” McCleary told me, choosing his words carefully. “This thing would move pretty quickly.”

As a result of their potential impact, these draft orders—at one point presumably kept under lock and key in the White House, nowadays probably maintained in highly secret digital files—have become as totemic and mysterious a symbol of presidential power as the nuclear football. He who has access to the nuclear codes can order the destruction of the world; he who has access to the PEADs—and can convince security forces that these PEADs are in fact genuine and legitimate and that orders to implement them should be followed even if they place the implementers in violation of the law—can order a sudden upending of America’s 250-year constitutional system of governance. In the hands of a man like Trump, facing a calamitous rejection from the electorate, such orders, if followed through on by law enforcement, security agents, and the military, could do untold damage to American democracy.

Column

 /

 Sasha Abramsky

Feature

 /

 The Nation

Column

 /

 Kate Wagner

Both Medish and McCleary believe the warning signs are flashing red that Trump could attempt to subvert the mechanisms of, and confidence in, the midterm voting process over the next two months—what Medish called, in a Freedom Media Watch presentation this week, “pre-delegitimizing the election.” Then, if the Republicans still lose, they believe that between November and January Trump could attempt to prevent the counting of votes, order the seizure of ballot boxes, try to invoke the Insurrection Act, invoke “commander-in-chief powers” domestically, and, if all else fails, use PEADs in an effort to take control of the electoral process and stifle dissent. “It’s a question of connecting the dots,” Medish said to me. “This is the devil’s accordion.”

Medish and McCleary worry that Trump could use PEADs to attempt to silence critics in the media and other institutions and to order the detention of political opponents and those considered “terrorists” under the expansive language of NSPM-7. They are deeply concerned that the Department of Homeland Security and agencies such as ICE have built an incarceration infrastructure that could be flipped from being targeted at immigrants to also being used against the regime’s political opponents. “These are extreme scenarios,” Medish said. “But knowing all we know about this presidency, it would be naïve to completely discount extreme scenarios and desperate acts.”

At the Brennan Center for Justice’s Liberty and National Security Program, senior director Liza Goitein also thinks it possible that Trump will invoke a national emergency and then attempt to use that declaration to attack the election process. There are, she says, 137 provisions in federal laws that could be activated in the event of his declaring a national emergency in addition to the PEADs that exist outside the legislative framework. Goitein does, however, believe that the courts would intervene to strike down patently unconstitutional actions, even in the context of a declared national emergency. The Supreme Court could do this without weighing in on whether Trump was correct in declaring the emergency in the first place. That, she says, is how the Supreme Court has reacted in the four cases, including tariff implementation, in which Trump’s actions occurred within the context of a declared national emergency. In each of those cases, the Supreme Court ruled that the laws Trump was relying on didn’t in fact give him the powers that he was claiming. As a consequence, Goitein remains cautiously optimistic that, despite Trump’s best efforts, free and fair elections will take place in November, that “people who have a vested interest in defending democracy are ready to defend the legal right to vote,” and that courts will rapidly swat down moves to attack that right.

Medish and McCleary are far less confident that the courts will hold. They told me that they are penning these warnings now not to instill a sense of fatalism or despair, but so that a) politicians and elections officials can approach the coming months with eyes wide open; and b) the populace as a whole can more fully understand the stakes and how important it is to deliver Republicans an electoral defeat so large that it becomes politically impossible for the administration to activate PEADs or other emergency powers to do an end run around the GOP and Trump’s humiliation.

The public’s role in this is critical since Trump, Medish explained, could argue that in a national-emergency situation (defined largely by himself), he needs to activate previously unused executive powers to protect the homeland, “and to do that, he’s going to need to suspend statutes, due process rights, and so forth. It’s analogous to Lincoln and the suspension of habeas corpus.” At that point, worries Medish, all the power resides with the executive. “They basically say, ‘Sue me, take it to court,’” and the courts then spend so long deliberating over it that by the time judges reach decisions, the damage—in this case to the election process—has already been done. “The courts have a huge difficulty stopping executive action on national security in real time.”

And, Medish and McCleary say, if the courts can’t stop Trump and the GOP-led Congress won’t stop him, that places the burden on an aroused and enraged public to push back against Trump and his instincts to declare an emergency so as to preserve his hold on power. To vote as if the future of their democracy depends on it. And to be willing to protest, even to engage in civil disobedience, should Trump arrogate extraordinary powers to himself. “Look, we are in a difficult situation,” McCleary concluded. “People understand how dangerous it is, but they don’t understand all the elements of the danger.”

title: Trump moves to strip tax-exempt status from schools that consider race
